author: A Robot
objectives: Determine steric number from a Lewis structure by counting bonding domains and lone pairs around a central atom.
Predict electron-domain geometry from steric number for linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral arrangements.
Distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry when lone pairs are present.
Explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs and predict the direction of bond-angle deviations.
Apply VSEPR predictions to real and unfamiliar molecules and compare predicted geometries with observed molecular structures.

modules.moduleName: Scene 1 — VSEPR from a Lewis Structure
modules.description: Introduces the VSEPR model, electron domains, and how a flat Lewis structure provides the input for predicting a three-dimensional molecular shape.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Define an electron domain as a bond region or lone pair around a central atom.
Count electron domains from a Lewis structure, treating each single, double, or triple bond as one domain.
Explain that VSEPR converts Lewis-structure information into a three-dimensional prediction.
instructions: Place the lab on a clear tabletop or floor area in front of you.
Read the Lewis structure panel and compare it to the domains appearing around the central atom.
Use Next to move through the guided explanation.

components.text: Count domains on the central atom

clips.changeMeaning: The central atom and its label appear as the focus for all later electron-domain counting and shape prediction.
clips.narration: Welcome to VSEPR theory: valence shell electron pair repulsion. Around a central atom, bonding pairs and lone pairs repel one another, and the molecule adopts the arrangement that places these electron domains as far apart as possible.

components.text: Single, double, or triple bond = 1 domain

clips.changeMeaning: The water Lewis structure panel is introduced beside the 3D atom to connect flat symbolic chemistry with spatial prediction.
clips.narration: VSEPR begins with a Lewis structure. A Lewis structure is drawn flat, but it tells us how many electron domains surround the central atom.

components.text: H2O: 2 bonds + 2 lone pairs = steric number 4

clips.changeMeaning: Representative bonding and lone-pair regions appear around the central atom to show what is being counted in the Lewis structure.
clips.narration: For water, oxygen has two O-H bonding domains and two lone-pair domains. That gives a steric number of four.

clips.changeMeaning: The domains enlarge slightly and the label changes from counting to predicting, preparing students for geometric rearrangement.
clips.narration: The VSEPR task is to take that steric number and decide how the domains arrange in three dimensions. The next scene shows the minimum-repulsion principle directly.

modules.moduleName: Scene 2 — Minimum Repulsion with 2, 3, and 4 Domains
modules.description: Shows electron domains moving from unstable starting positions into linear, trigonal planar, and tetrahedral electron-domain geometries.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Relate electron-domain repulsion to maximum spatial separation.
Identify linear, trigonal planar, and tetrahedral electron-domain geometries.
Associate ideal angles of 180°, 120°, and 109.5° with steric numbers 2, 3, and 4.
instructions: Observe the starting positions before each geometry settles.
Compare the final arrangement to the displayed angle label.
Notice when the arrangement must become three-dimensional.

clips.changeMeaning: Two domains are placed near one another and a repulsion vector appears to visualize the force that will separate them.
clips.narration: Two electron domains that start close together repel strongly. The repulsion arrow indicates that they will move apart.

clips.changeMeaning: The two electron domains move to opposite sides of the central atom and the arrow fades because the linear arrangement is stable.
clips.narration: The minimum-repulsion arrangement for two domains is linear. The domains settle 180 degrees apart.

clips.changeMeaning: A third domain appears and all three domains move into a planar triangular arrangement around the central atom.
clips.narration: When a third domain is added, the domains spread out in one plane. The trigonal planar arrangement has ideal 120 degree angles.

clips.changeMeaning: A fourth domain appears above the plane and all domains shift to a three-dimensional tetrahedral arrangement.
clips.narration: Four domains cannot maximize separation in a flat plane. They form a tetrahedron, with ideal angles of about 109.5 degrees.

modules.moduleName: Scene 3 — The Five- and Six-Domain Catalog
modules.description: Completes the electron-domain geometry catalog with trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral geometries and displays a summary panel of all five fundamental arrangements.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify trigonal bipyramidal geometry for steric number five.
Differentiate axial and equatorial positions in trigonal bipyramidal geometry.
Identify octahedral geometry for steric number six and summarize all five electron-domain geometries.
instructions: Walk around the model to see the axial and equatorial directions.
Compare the 90° and 120° relationships in the five-domain arrangement.
Use the final panel as a reference for all steric numbers from two to six.

clips.changeMeaning: Three equatorial domains are shown first so the student can recognize the planar portion of trigonal bipyramidal geometry.
clips.narration: For steric number five, three positions begin in an equatorial plane. These equatorial domains are separated by 120 degrees.

clips.changeMeaning: The axial top and bottom domains appear, completing the five-domain trigonal bipyramidal arrangement.
clips.narration: Adding two axial domains above and below the plane gives trigonal bipyramidal geometry. Axial-to-equatorial angles are 90 degrees.

clips.changeMeaning: The five-domain model is restaged as six symmetric directions, using the same lobes to show an octahedral scaffold.
clips.narration: Six electron domains form octahedral geometry. The domains point toward six opposite directions, and adjacent positions are 90 degrees apart.

clips.changeMeaning: A summary panel appears below the model, consolidating domain counts, geometry names, and characteristic angles.
clips.narration: The complete electron-domain catalog is linear for two domains, trigonal planar for three, tetrahedral for four, trigonal bipyramidal for five, and octahedral for six.

modules.moduleName: Scene 4 — Electron-Domain Geometry vs Molecular Geometry
modules.description: Uses methane, ammonia, and water to show that the electron-domain scaffold can remain tetrahedral while the molecular geometry changes when lone pairs replace atoms.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Distinguish the arrangement of all electron domains from the arrangement of atoms only.
Predict trigonal pyramidal geometry for AX3E and bent geometry for AX2E2.
Explain why lone pairs are included in electron-domain geometry but omitted from molecular-geometry names.
instructions: Watch the top and rear bonded atoms change into lone-pair clouds.
Compare the electron-domain geometry label with the molecular-geometry label.
Remember that molecular geometry names only atom positions.

clips.changeMeaning: The all-bonding methane model establishes the reference case where electron-domain and molecular geometries match.
clips.narration: Methane has four bonding domains and no lone pairs on carbon. Its electron-domain geometry is tetrahedral, and its molecular geometry is also tetrahedral.

components.text: NH3: EDG tetrahedral | MG trigonal pyramidal

clips.changeMeaning: One hydrogen position is replaced by a lone-pair cloud and the shape trace changes from tetrahedral to trigonal pyramidal.
clips.narration: In ammonia, one tetrahedral position is occupied by a lone pair. The electron-domain geometry is still tetrahedral, but the atoms alone form a trigonal pyramid.

clips.changeMeaning: A second tetrahedral position becomes a lone-pair cloud, leaving only two atoms to define the bent molecular geometry.
clips.narration: Water has two bonding domains and two lone pairs. Its electron-domain geometry is tetrahedral, but its molecular geometry is bent.

components.text: EDG counts domains | MG traces atoms only

clips.changeMeaning: The lone-pair clouds expand and the label changes to the general rule separating electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry.
clips.narration: Electron-domain geometry counts all bonding and lone-pair domains. Molecular geometry names only the arrangement of atoms, even though lone pairs help determine that arrangement.

modules.moduleName: Scene 5 — Lone Pairs Compress Bond Angles
modules.description: Compares methane, ammonia, and water side by side to show how larger lone-pair domains compress the remaining bonding angles.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Compare bond angles of CH4, NH3, and H2O.
Explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding domains.
Predict that bonding angles shrink as more lone pairs are added near them.
instructions: Compare the three molecules from left to right.
Look for larger lone-pair clouds on ammonia and water.
Use the overlay panel to compare the decreasing H-X-H angle.

clips.changeMeaning: Three comparable molecule models are shown side by side with a single label giving their characteristic bond angles.
clips.narration: Methane, ammonia, and water all come from a steric number four electron-domain arrangement, but their observed bond angles are different.

components.text: Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs

clips.changeMeaning: Ammonia and water are enlarged and retextured to emphasize their lone-pair clouds occupying more angular space.
clips.narration: Lone pairs are held by only the central atom rather than shared between two nuclei, so they spread out more and repel bonding domains more strongly.

components.text: More lone pairs → smaller bonding angle

clips.changeMeaning: An overlay panel appears to show the angle sequence from methane to ammonia to water in one comparison view.
clips.narration: The overlay compares the central bond angles directly. As the number of lone pairs increases, the H-X-H angle decreases.

components.text: Prediction rule: ideal angle, then adjust for lone pairs

clips.changeMeaning: The comparison is reframed as a reusable prediction rule for students to apply in later molecule examples.
clips.narration: When estimating angles, start with the ideal electron-domain angle and reduce bonding angles next to lone pairs. More lone pairs generally mean greater compression.

modules.description: Displays real molecules spanning all five electron-domain geometries and several lone-pair-derived molecular geometries.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Apply VSEPR to CO2, BF3, CH4, PF5, SF6, NH3, H2O, and XeF4.
Name electron-domain geometry, molecular geometry, and approximate angles for representative molecules.
Compare predicted VSEPR shapes with observed molecular structures.
instructions: Inspect each molecule station and its Lewis count panel.
For each station, identify bonding domains, lone pairs, electron-domain geometry, and molecular geometry.
Advance through the narrated gallery highlights.

clips.changeMeaning: All molecule stations are visible together so students can recognize the breadth of VSEPR examples in one spatial gallery.
clips.narration: This gallery connects VSEPR predictions to real molecules. Each station displays a Lewis structure, a 3D model, and the central atom's domain count.

clips.changeMeaning: The CO2, BF3, and CH4 stations enlarge to emphasize the steric number two, three, and four all-bonding examples.
clips.narration: Carbon dioxide is linear with two domains. Boron trifluoride is trigonal planar with three domains. Methane is tetrahedral with four bonding domains.

clips.changeMeaning: The PF5 and SF6 stations enlarge while earlier examples return to normal size, focusing attention on steric numbers five and six.
clips.narration: Phosphorus pentafluoride has five bonding domains and trigonal bipyramidal geometry. Sulfur hexafluoride has six bonding domains and octahedral geometry.

clips.changeMeaning: The NH3, H2O, and XeF4 stations enlarge to highlight common lone-pair-containing molecular geometries.
clips.narration: Ammonia is trigonal pyramidal, water is bent, and xenon tetrafluoride is square planar. In each case, lone pairs change the molecular geometry while still occupying electron-domain positions.

clips.changeMeaning: All stations return to matching size and the panel changes to the universal VSEPR workflow used for every example.
clips.narration: Across the gallery, the workflow is the same: count domains, identify electron-domain geometry, account for lone pairs, and name the molecular geometry.

modules.moduleName: Scene 7 — Prediction Activity: Drag the Domains
modules.description: Provides an interactive-style domain arrangement activity where students place domains into target VSEPR geometries and then compare with the ideal snap positions.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Construct correct minimum-repulsion arrangements for steric numbers two through six.
Recognize correct angular relationships in each electron-domain geometry.
Place lone pairs in electron-domain positions while naming molecular geometry from atoms alone.
instructions: Drag the domain objects around the central atom when prompted by the activity system.
Try to match the target angles described on the prompt panel.
After each challenge, compare your arrangement to the snapped ideal positions.

clips.changeMeaning: Four domains start in loose nonideal positions and the prompt panel identifies the tetrahedral target for steric number four.
clips.narration: Your first challenge has four electron domains. Arrange them to minimize repulsion. The target is tetrahedral, with angles near 109.5 degrees.

clips.changeMeaning: The four movable domains snap into ideal tetrahedral positions and a green glow confirms the correct geometry.
clips.narration: Correct. Four domains snap into a tetrahedral arrangement. This is the electron-domain geometry for steric number four.

clips.changeMeaning: Additional domains appear and the prompt indicates a sequence of all-bonding geometry challenges across steric numbers two through six.
clips.narration: The same idea works for two, three, five, and six domains: linear, trigonal planar, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral geometries.

clips.changeMeaning: One of the four domains changes texture into a lone pair, prompting the student to preserve tetrahedral domain positions while naming a different molecular geometry.
clips.narration: Now arrange four domains where one is a lone pair. The electron-domain geometry is still tetrahedral, but three bonded atoms and one lone pair produce trigonal pyramidal molecular geometry.

clips.changeMeaning: The mixed bonding and lone-pair domains snap into the tetrahedral scaffold and the prompt panel confirms the EDG and MG names.
clips.narration: Correct. The lone pair occupies one tetrahedral position. The electron-domain geometry is tetrahedral, but the atoms form a trigonal pyramid.

modules.moduleName: Scene 8 — Prediction Activity: Choose the Correct Shape
modules.description: Students analyze Lewis structures for unfamiliar molecules and ions, then choose the matching 3D molecular geometry from candidate options.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Determine steric number and lone-pair count for SF4, ClF3, BrF5, and I3−.
Recognize seesaw, T-shaped, square pyramidal, and linear geometries that arise from lone pairs.
Justify VSEPR predictions using the sequence count domains, identify EDG, account for lone pairs, and name MG.
instructions: Start by reading the Lewis structure panel.
Count bonding domains and lone pairs on the central atom.
Compare the answer options and then review the feedback panel.

clips.changeMeaning: The SF4 Lewis structure and four candidate geometry cards appear to initiate a VSEPR selection challenge.
clips.narration: Challenge one is sulfur tetrafluoride, SF4. Count four S-F bonds and one lone pair on sulfur. Steric number five gives a trigonal bipyramidal electron-domain geometry.

clips.changeMeaning: The seesaw option is highlighted and the feedback panel displays the reasoning from steric number five to seesaw geometry.
clips.narration: The correct molecular geometry is seesaw. In a trigonal bipyramidal scaffold, the lone pair occupies an equatorial position, leaving four atoms in a seesaw shape.

clips.changeMeaning: The challenge changes to ClF3 and the T-shaped answer is emphasized with the same count, arrange, account, name reasoning.
clips.narration: For chlorine trifluoride, ClF3, count three bonding domains and two lone pairs. Steric number five again gives trigonal bipyramidal electron-domain geometry, and the atoms form a T shape.

clips.changeMeaning: The challenge switches to BrF5 and highlights a square pyramidal option derived from an octahedral electron-domain arrangement.
clips.narration: For bromine pentafluoride, BrF5, five bonds and one lone pair give steric number six. The electron-domain geometry is octahedral, and the molecular geometry is square pyramidal.

clips.changeMeaning: The final challenge displays I3− and highlights a linear answer resulting from three equatorial lone pairs in a trigonal bipyramidal scaffold.
clips.narration: For triiodide, I3 minus, the central iodine has two bonding domains and three lone pairs. The electron-domain geometry is trigonal bipyramidal, but the atoms are opposite each other, so molecular geometry is linear.

modules.description: Closes the lab by reviewing the minimum-repulsion principle, the electron-domain geometry catalog, molecular geometry, lone-pair angle effects, and the final prediction workflow.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Summarize the complete VSEPR prediction process from Lewis structure to molecular geometry.
Recall the five electron-domain geometries and the role of lone pairs.
Use a final workflow checklist for future VSEPR problems.
instructions: Read each highlighted recap panel.
Use the final workflow as a checklist for homework and exam questions.
Replay any earlier scene if a step feels uncertain.

components.text: VSEPR Recap: Count → Arrange → Name → Refine

clips.changeMeaning: The recap panel highlights the minimum-repulsion principle and the first orb enlarges to mark the starting concept.
clips.narration: VSEPR begins with the minimum-repulsion principle: electron domains repel one another and arrange to maximize separation around the central atom.

clips.changeMeaning: The panel changes to the geometry table and the second orb enlarges to emphasize steric number to electron-domain geometry.
clips.narration: The five electron-domain geometries are linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral for steric numbers two through six.

clips.changeMeaning: The panel switches to lone-pair-derived molecular geometries and the third orb enlarges to show the EDG versus MG step.
clips.narration: Electron-domain geometry counts all domains, while molecular geometry names the atoms only. Lone pairs can create bent, trigonal pyramidal, seesaw, T-shaped, square pyramidal, and square planar shapes.

clips.changeMeaning: The angle-compression recap appears and the fourth orb enlarges to mark the refinement of ideal bond angles.
clips.narration: Lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, so they compress nearby bond angles. Water is smaller than ammonia, and ammonia is smaller than methane.

components.text: You can now predict VSEPR molecular shapes

clips.changeMeaning: All workflow orbs enlarge and the final panel displays a reusable checklist for future VSEPR prediction problems.
clips.narration: For any new molecule, draw or read the Lewis structure, count domains, identify electron-domain geometry, account for lone pairs, name molecular geometry, and estimate bond angles.
